lead: A chain drive pulls a roller chain over two sprockets. The rollers sit in tooth gaps, so the chain cannot slip and the velocity ratio is fixed by tooth counts. It carries more torque than a belt in the same space, works at high temperature and in oil, and is common on motorcycles, industrial conveyors and engine camshafts. The cost is chordal action, which makes the speed pulse and adds impact at engagement; separately, the pin-bush hinge slides under load, so the chain must be lubricated and it wears as pitch elongates.
prereq: You need: 6.1 for the place of a chain among flexible drives, and 6.3 for the service-factor habit.

blocks.text: A roller chain is a set of short links. Each link has two pins pressed into outer plates. Bushes on the pins carry rollers, and inner plates hold the bush ends. The roller touches the sprocket tooth. Pin, bush and roller make a hinge, so the chain bends around the sprocket without sliding.

Types: roller chain (bush roller chain) for power transmission; silent or inverted-tooth chain, where shaped plates engage the sprocket teeth and there are no rollers, used at high speed and low noise; block chain, simple cast blocks for low speed; detachable chain, hooked links for farm machinery.

Standard designation fixes pitch p (distance between pin centres), roller diameter and inner width. ISO 08B has p = 12.7 mm. ISO 10B has p = 15.875 mm. ANSI 40 and ANSI 50 are the US-series chains with the same two pitches. Give the standard number when ordering: two chains with the same pitch can have different roller sizes and will not fit the same sprocket.

Let Z₁ be teeth on the small sprocket, Z₂ on the large, p pitch in metres, N₁ small-sprocket speed in rev/min. The exact mean chain speed from the polygon perimeter is v = Z₁ p N₁/60, while π d₁ N₁/60 is the speed of a point on the pitch circle; the two differ by less than 1% for Z ≥ 17. State which one you use.
v = Z₁ p N₁ / 60 ≈ π d₁ N₁ / 60
blocks.where: v is pitch-line speed in m/s; Z₁ is teeth on the small sprocket; p is pitch in m; N₁ is its speed in rev/min; d₁ is pitch diameter in m.

blocks.text: Pitch diameter is d = p/sin(180°/Z). This is the circle through roller centres, not the tip circle. A 19-tooth 08B sprocket has d = 12.7/sin 9.474° = 77.16 mm.

blocks.where: d is pitch diameter; p is pitch; Z is number of teeth. Use degrees in the calculator.

blocks.text: Chordal action: the chain leaves the sprocket as a polygon. Link speed rises and falls between v and v cos(180°/Z). The fractional fall is 1 − cos(180°/Z). At Z = 11 it is 4.0%; at Z = 19 it is 1.36%. Few teeth also mean a smaller pitch diameter, so the same torque gives a higher chain tension. Use at least 17 teeth; 19 or more for smooth running.

blocks.where: fractional variation of chain speed for a sprocket with Z teeth; multiply by 100 for percent.

blocks.text: Chain length in pitches for centre distance C: L = 2C/p + (Z₁+Z₂)/2 + ((Z₂−Z₁)/(2π))² p/C. Round L up to an even number of links, because an odd count needs an offset link.

blocks.where: L is chain length in pitches; C is centre distance; p is pitch; Z₁ and Z₂ are teeth. Round L up to an even number of links.

blocks.text: Failure modes: fatigue of the link plates under the fluctuating tension, and impact fatigue of rollers and bushes at each engagement with the sprocket; wear of pins and bushes, which increases pitch and elongates the chain; roller wear, which reduces roller diameter and damages tooth seating; roller breakage; galling when the oil film breaks down under high pressure; and jumping the tooth when elongation is too large. A common replacement limit is about 1.5% elongation; check the manufacturer's figure.

items: Find service factor Ks from driver, driven machine and hours per day.
Choose Z₁ ≥ 17 (19 for smooth running), Z₂ = i Z₁, where i is the velocity ratio.
From the chain rating chart, read the power rating at N₁ for each chain number; pick the first chain with rating ≥ design power.
Choose centre distance C between about 30p and 50p; compute L, round to even links, then find the exact C for those links.
Check lubrication method and shaft loads.

blocks.text: Lubrication: brush or manual oiling for low speed; drip feed; bath or disc lubrication for enclosed drives; spray for high speed. Oil must reach the pin-bush hinge. Grease is for sealed motorcycle chains, not for high-speed industrial chains. Leave a small slack-side sag, roughly 2% of centre distance; too tight a chain overloads shafts and bearings. Use an idler or move the motor to adjust.

figure.caption: Percentage speed variation 100(1 − cos(180/Z)) falls as the small sprocket gains teeth. At 11 teeth it is about 4.0%; at 19 teeth it is 1.36%, which is why 19 teeth is the smooth-running minimum.

spec.aria: A falling curve of percentage chain speed variation against the number of teeth on the small sprocket, about 4 percent at 11 teeth and 1.4 percent at 19 teeth.

examples.question: A 7.5 kW, 1000 rpm motor drives a compressor through a single-strand 08B roller chain. Pitch p = 12.7 mm, Z₁ = 19, Z₂ = 38, centre distance C = 500 mm. The catalogue breaking load is 18 kN. Find the pitch diameter of the small sprocket, the chain speed, the chain tension, the factor of safety on breaking load, the chain length in pitches and links, and the speed variation. Neglect centrifugal tension and sag.
steps: Factor of safety: FoS = breaking load / F = 18000/1856 = 9.7.
Links: round up to an even number, so use 108 links.
examples.answer: d₁ = 77.16 mm, v = 4.04 m/s, F = 1856 N, FoS = 9.7, L = 107.5 pitches rounded to 108 links, and speed variation = 1.36%. This FoS only shows the chain will not break in tension; whether 08B is acceptable must be checked against its catalogue power rating at 1000 rpm with the service factor applied.
examples.check:
import math
p = 12.7
Z1 = 19
Z2 = 38
C = 500.0
N1 = 1000.0
P = 7500.0
Q = 18000.0
d1 = p / math.sin(math.pi / Z1)
v = math.pi * (d1 / 1000.0) * N1 / 60.0
F = P / v
fos = Q / F
L = 2*C/p + (Z1+Z2)/2 + ((Z2-Z1)/(2*math.pi))**2 * p/C
links = math.ceil(L/2.0)*2
var = 100.0*(1.0 - math.cos(math.pi/Z1))
print(round(d1, 2))
print(round(v, 2))
print(round(F))
print(round(fos, 1))
print(round(L, 1))
print(links)
print(round(var, 2))

traps: Rounding chain length to an odd number of links. An odd count needs an offset link, which is weaker; round up to an even number and recompute the exact centre distance for that link count (it comes out slightly larger, about 3 mm more here), or keep C and take up the small extra slack with an idler or by moving the motor.
Using the tip diameter instead of the pitch diameter in d = p/sin(180°/Z). The chain sits on the pitch circle; tip diameter gives a false speed and false tension.
Choosing a chain from motor kW alone. The catalogue rating must be compared with design power = service factor × motor power.
Writing speed variation as cos(180°/Z) instead of 1 − cos(180°/Z). At 19 teeth the variation is 1.36%, not 98.6%.
Setting a chain as tight as a V-belt. A chain needs a little slack for polygon action; too tight overloads shaft bearings.

quiz.q: Name the parts of a roller chain link and say which one touches the sprocket tooth.
quiz.a: Pin, bush, roller, inner plate, outer plate; the roller touches the tooth.

quiz.q: Why is the velocity ratio of a chain drive exact, while a belt drive can slip?
quiz.a: The rollers sit in the tooth gaps, so the chain is pulled by positive contact and cannot slip. A belt depends on friction and can slip when overloaded.

quiz.q: An 08B chain (p = 12.7 mm) runs on a 17-tooth sprocket at 800 rpm. Find pitch diameter and average chain speed.
Why specify at least 19 teeth on the small sprocket for a smooth high-speed drive?
quiz.a: Speed variation is 1 − cos(180/Z). At 19 teeth it is 1.36%; at 11 teeth it is 4.0%. More teeth reduce pulsation, noise and wear, and increase pitch diameter, which lowers chain tension for the same torque.

quiz.q: A drive has design power 11 kW at 720 rpm. A 10B chain is rated 12 kW at 720 rpm. Is the chain acceptable?
quiz.a: Yes. The rating 12 kW is greater than the design power 11 kW; service factor is already in the design power.

quiz.q: Why is an offset link avoided in a roller chain?
quiz.a: It is used to close an odd number of links. The offset link uses a cranked plate, so the pull is eccentric and the plate carries bending on top of tension; it is the weakest link and a common failure point.

quiz.q: A chain has elongated 2% and jumps teeth. Give the cause and the remedy.
quiz.a: Wear at pins and bushes increases pitch; the chain sits high on the teeth and skips. Replace chain and worn sprockets, restore correct sag and improve lubrication.

quiz.q: Why does a chain drive need lubrication even though it does not rely on friction?
quiz.a: The pin-bush hinge has sliding contact under high pressure. Oil prevents metal-to-metal wear, galling and corrosion, and carries heat away.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry, roller chains are selected from manufacturer catalogues that give power ratings for each chain number, speed and lubrication class. High-speed engines use silent chains and toothed belts; conveyors use heavy roller chains with attachments. Newer work fits vibration and acoustic sensors to chain drives to estimate wear from the changing polygon frequency. Search for 'chain drive selection ISO 606', 'silent chain vs roller chain' and 'chain wear elongation limit'.
